scene.label: Act 4, Scene 1
scene.title: SCENE I. The Forest of Arden

lines.text: I prithee, pretty youth, let me be better acquainted with thee.
lines.plainText: I prithee pretty youth let me be better acquainted with thee

lines.text: They say you are a melancholy fellow.
lines.plainText: They say you are a melancholy fellow

lines.text: I am so; I do love it better than laughing.
lines.plainText: I am so I do love it better than laughing

lines.text: Those that are in extremity of either are abominable fellows, and betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards.
lines.plainText: Those that are in extremity of either are abominable fellows and betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards

lines.text: Why, 'tis good to be sad and say nothing.
lines.plainText: Why 'tis good to be sad and say nothing

lines.text: Why then, 'tis good to be a post.
lines.plainText: Why then 'tis good to be a post

lines.text: I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is emulation; nor the musician's, which is fantastical; nor the courtier's, which is proud; nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is politic; nor the lady's, which is nice; nor the lover's, which is all these; but it is a melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and indeed the sundry contemplation of my travels, in which my often rumination wraps me in a most humorous sadness.
lines.plainText: I have neither the scholar's melancholy which is emulation nor the musician's which is fantastical nor the courtier's which is proud nor the soldier's which is ambitious nor the lawyer's which is politic nor the lady's which is nice nor the lover's which is all these but it is a melancholy of mine own compounded of many simples extracted from many objects and indeed the sundry contemplation of my travels in which my often rumination wraps me in a most humorous sadness

lines.text: A traveller! By my faith, you have great reason to be sad. I fear you have sold your own lands to see other men's. Then to have seen much and to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.
lines.plainText: A traveller By my faith you have great reason to be sad I fear you have sold your own lands to see other men's Then to have seen much and to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands

lines.text: Yes, I have gained my experience.
lines.plainText: Yes I have gained my experience

lines.text: And your experience makes you sad. I had rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad—and to travel for it too.
lines.plainText: And your experience makes you sad I had rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sadand to travel for it too

lines.text: Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind!
lines.plainText: Good day and happiness dear Rosalind

lines.text: Nay, then, God be wi' you, an you talk in blank verse.
lines.plainText: Nay then God be wi' you an you talk in blank verse

lines.text: Farewell, Monsieur Traveller. Look you lisp and wear strange suits; disable all the benefits of your own country; be out of love with your nativity, and almost chide God for making you that countenance you are, or I will scarce think you have swam in a gondola.
lines.plainText: Farewell Monsieur Traveller Look you lisp and wear strange suits disable all the benefits of your own country be out of love with your nativity and almost chide God for making you that countenance you are or I will scarce think you have swam in a gondola

lines.text: My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.
lines.plainText: My fair Rosalind I come within an hour of my promise

lines.text: Break an hour's promise in love? He that will divide a minute into a thousand parts, and break but a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid hath clapped him o' the shoulder, but I'll warrant him heart-whole.
lines.plainText: Break an hour's promise in love He that will divide a minute into a thousand parts and break but a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love it may be said of him that Cupid hath clapped him o' the shoulder but I'll warrant him heartwhole

lines.text: Pardon me, dear Rosalind.
lines.plainText: Pardon me dear Rosalind

lines.text: Nay, an you be so tardy, come no more in my sight. I had as lief be wooed of a snail.
lines.plainText: Nay an you be so tardy come no more in my sight I had as lief be wooed of a snail

lines.text: Of a snail?
lines.plainText: Of a snail

lines.text: Ay, of a snail, for though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his head—a better jointure, I think, than you make a woman. Besides, he brings his destiny with him.
lines.plainText: Ay of a snail for though he comes slowly he carries his house on his heada better jointure I think than you make a woman Besides he brings his destiny with him

lines.text: What's that?
lines.plainText: What's that

lines.text: Why, horns, which such as you are fain to be beholding to your wives for. But he comes armed in his fortune and prevents the slander of his wife.
lines.plainText: Why horns which such as you are fain to be beholding to your wives for But he comes armed in his fortune and prevents the slander of his wife

lines.text: Virtue is no horn-maker and my Rosalind is virtuous.
lines.plainText: Virtue is no hornmaker and my Rosalind is virtuous

lines.text: And I am your Rosalind.
lines.plainText: And I am your Rosalind

lines.text: It pleases him to call you so, but he hath a Rosalind of a better leer than you.
lines.plainText: It pleases him to call you so but he hath a Rosalind of a better leer than you

lines.text: Come, woo me, woo me, for now I am in a holiday humour, and like enough to consent. What would you say to me now, an I were your very, very Rosalind?
lines.plainText: Come woo me woo me for now I am in a holiday humour and like enough to consent What would you say to me now an I were your very very Rosalind

lines.text: I would kiss before I spoke.
lines.plainText: I would kiss before I spoke

lines.text: Nay, you were better speak first, and when you were gravelled for lack of matter, you might take occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when they are out, they will spit; and for lovers lacking—God warn us—matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.
lines.plainText: Nay you were better speak first and when you were gravelled for lack of matter you might take occasion to kiss Very good orators when they are out they will spit and for lovers lackingGod warn usmatter the cleanliest shift is to kiss

lines.text: How if the kiss be denied?
lines.plainText: How if the kiss be denied

lines.text: Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.
lines.plainText: Then she puts you to entreaty and there begins new matter

lines.text: Who could be out, being before his beloved mistress?
lines.plainText: Who could be out being before his beloved mistress

lines.text: Marry, that should you, if I were your mistress, or I should think my honesty ranker than my wit.
lines.plainText: Marry that should you if I were your mistress or I should think my honesty ranker than my wit

lines.text: What, of my suit?
lines.plainText: What of my suit

lines.text: Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am not I your Rosalind?
lines.plainText: Not out of your apparel and yet out of your suit Am not I your Rosalind

lines.text: I take some joy to say you are because I would be talking of her.
lines.plainText: I take some joy to say you are because I would be talking of her

lines.text: Well, in her person, I say I will not have you.
lines.plainText: Well in her person I say I will not have you

lines.text: Then, in mine own person, I die.
lines.plainText: Then in mine own person I die

lines.text: No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person, videlicet, in a love-cause. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club, yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander, he would have lived many a fair year though Hero had turned nun, if it had not been for a hot midsummer night; for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and, being taken with the cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of that age found it was Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies. Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
lines.plainText: No faith die by attorney The poor world is almost six thousand years old and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person videlicet in a lovecause Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club yet he did what he could to die before and he is one of the patterns of love Leander he would have lived many a fair year though Hero had turned nun if it had not been for a hot midsummer night for good youth he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and being taken with the cramp was drowned and the foolish chroniclers of that age found it was Hero of Sestos But these are all lies Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them but not for love

lines.text: I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind, for I protest her frown might kill me.
lines.plainText: I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind for I protest her frown might kill me

lines.text: By this hand, it will not kill a fly. But come, now I will be your Rosalind in a more coming-on disposition, and ask me what you will, I will grant it.
lines.plainText: By this hand it will not kill a fly But come now I will be your Rosalind in a more comingon disposition and ask me what you will I will grant it

lines.text: Then love me, Rosalind.
lines.plainText: Then love me Rosalind

lines.text: Yes, faith, will I, Fridays and Saturdays and all.
lines.plainText: Yes faith will I Fridays and Saturdays and all

lines.text: And wilt thou have me?
lines.plainText: And wilt thou have me

lines.text: Ay, and twenty such.
lines.plainText: Ay and twenty such

lines.text: What sayest thou?
lines.plainText: What sayest thou

lines.text: Are you not good?
lines.plainText: Are you not good

lines.text: I hope so.
lines.plainText: I hope so

lines.text: Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?—Come, sister, you shall be the priest and marry us.—Give me your hand, Orlando.—What do you say, sister?
lines.plainText: Why then can one desire too much of a good thingCome sister you shall be the priest and marry usGive me your hand OrlandoWhat do you say sister

lines.text: Pray thee, marry us.
lines.plainText: Pray thee marry us

lines.text: I cannot say the words.
lines.plainText: I cannot say the words

lines.text: You must begin "Will you, Orlando—"
lines.plainText: You must begin Will you Orlando

lines.text: Go to.—Will you, Orlando, have to wife this Rosalind?
lines.plainText: Go toWill you Orlando have to wife this Rosalind

lines.text: I will.
lines.plainText: I will

lines.text: Ay, but when?
lines.plainText: Ay but when

lines.text: Why now, as fast as she can marry us.
lines.plainText: Why now as fast as she can marry us

lines.text: Then you must say "I take thee, Rosalind, for wife."
lines.plainText: Then you must say I take thee Rosalind for wife

lines.text: I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.
lines.plainText: I take thee Rosalind for wife

lines.text: I might ask you for your commission. But I do take thee, Orlando, for my husband. There's a girl goes before the priest, and certainly a woman's thought runs before her actions.
lines.plainText: I might ask you for your commission But I do take thee Orlando for my husband There's a girl goes before the priest and certainly a woman's thought runs before her actions

lines.text: So do all thoughts. They are winged.
lines.plainText: So do all thoughts They are winged

lines.text: Now tell me how long you would have her after you have possessed her.
lines.plainText: Now tell me how long you would have her after you have possessed her

lines.text: For ever and a day.
lines.plainText: For ever and a day

lines.text: Say "a day" without the "ever." No, no, Orlando, men are April when they woo, December when they wed. Maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous of thee than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires than a monkey. I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I will do that when you are disposed to be merry. I will laugh like a hyena, and that when thou are inclined to sleep.
lines.plainText: Say a day without the ever No no Orlando men are April when they woo December when they wed Maids are May when they are maids but the sky changes when they are wives I will be more jealous of thee than a Barbary cockpigeon over his hen more clamorous than a parrot against rain more newfangled than an ape more giddy in my desires than a monkey I will weep for nothing like Diana in the fountain and I will do that when you are disposed to be merry I will laugh like a hyena and that when thou are inclined to sleep

lines.text: But will my Rosalind do so?
lines.plainText: But will my Rosalind do so

lines.text: By my life, she will do as I do.
lines.plainText: By my life she will do as I do

lines.text: O, but she is wise.
lines.plainText: O but she is wise

lines.text: Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The wiser, the waywarder. Make the doors upon a woman's wit, and it will out at the casement. Shut that, and 'twill out at the keyhole. Stop that, 'twill fly with the smoke out at the chimney.
lines.plainText: Or else she could not have the wit to do this The wiser the waywarder Make the doors upon a woman's wit and it will out at the casement Shut that and 'twill out at the keyhole Stop that 'twill fly with the smoke out at the chimney

lines.text: A man that had a wife with such a wit, he might say, "Wit, whither wilt?"
lines.plainText: A man that had a wife with such a wit he might say Wit whither wilt

lines.text: Nay, you might keep that check for it till you met your wife's wit going to your neighbour's bed.
lines.plainText: Nay you might keep that check for it till you met your wife's wit going to your neighbour's bed

lines.text: And what wit could wit have to excuse that?
lines.plainText: And what wit could wit have to excuse that

lines.text: Marry, to say she came to seek you there. You shall never take her without her answer unless you take her without her tongue. O, that woman that cannot make her fault her husband's occasion, let her never nurse her child herself, for she will breed it like a fool.
lines.plainText: Marry to say she came to seek you there You shall never take her without her answer unless you take her without her tongue O that woman that cannot make her fault her husband's occasion let her never nurse her child herself for she will breed it like a fool

lines.text: For these two hours, Rosalind, I will leave thee.
lines.plainText: For these two hours Rosalind I will leave thee

lines.text: Alas, dear love, I cannot lack thee two hours.
lines.plainText: Alas dear love I cannot lack thee two hours

lines.text: I must attend the Duke at dinner. By two o'clock I will be with thee again.
lines.plainText: I must attend the Duke at dinner By two o'clock I will be with thee again

lines.text: Ay, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would prove. My friends told me as much, and I thought no less. That flattering tongue of yours won me. 'Tis but one cast away, and so, come death! Two o'clock is your hour?
lines.plainText: Ay go your ways go your ways I knew what you would prove My friends told me as much and I thought no less That flattering tongue of yours won me 'Tis but one cast away and so come death Two o'clock is your hour

lines.text: Ay, sweet Rosalind.
lines.plainText: Ay sweet Rosalind

lines.text: By my troth, and in good earnest, and so God mend me, and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous, if you break one jot of your promise or come one minute behind your hour, I will think you the most pathetical break-promise, and the most hollow lover, and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind that may be chosen out of the gross band of the unfaithful. Therefore beware my censure, and keep your promise.
lines.plainText: By my troth and in good earnest and so God mend me and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous if you break one jot of your promise or come one minute behind your hour I will think you the most pathetical breakpromise and the most hollow lover and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind that may be chosen out of the gross band of the unfaithful Therefore beware my censure and keep your promise

lines.text: With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my Rosalind. So, adieu.
lines.plainText: With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my Rosalind So adieu

lines.text: Well, Time is the old justice that examines all such offenders, and let time try. Adieu.
lines.plainText: Well Time is the old justice that examines all such offenders and let time try Adieu

lines.text: You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate! We must have your doublet and hose plucked over your head and show the world what the bird hath done to her own nest.
lines.plainText: You have simply misused our sex in your loveprate We must have your doublet and hose plucked over your head and show the world what the bird hath done to her own nest

lines.text: O coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz, that thou didst know how many fathom deep I am in love! But it cannot be sounded; my affection hath an unknown bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.
lines.plainText: O coz coz coz my pretty little coz that thou didst know how many fathom deep I am in love But it cannot be sounded my affection hath an unknown bottom like the Bay of Portugal

lines.text: Or rather, bottomless, that as fast as you pour affection in, it runs out.
lines.plainText: Or rather bottomless that as fast as you pour affection in it runs out

lines.text: No, that same wicked bastard of Venus, that was begot of thought, conceived of spleen, and born of madness, that blind rascally boy that abuses everyone's eyes because his own are out, let him be judge how deep I am in love. I'll tell thee, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando. I'll go find a shadow and sigh till he come.
lines.plainText: No that same wicked bastard of Venus that was begot of thought conceived of spleen and born of madness that blind rascally boy that abuses everyone's eyes because his own are out let him be judge how deep I am in love I'll tell thee Aliena I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando I'll go find a shadow and sigh till he come

lines.text: And I'll sleep.
